title: Destructors and Object Lifetime
summary: A **destructor**, `~ClassName()`, runs automatically when an object's life ends. Use it to release what the object holds: files, memory, locks. Objects are destroyed in the **reverse** order of their creation.
ideas:
1. Create `Noisy` objects in a function, in a loop body and in a vector. Predict the output before running it.
2. Add a `static int` to `Noisy` that counts live objects: increment it in the constructor and decrement it in the destructor. (A preview of [[6.05 Static Members and Friends]].)
3. Give `Noisy` a member that is itself a `Noisy` and observe the order of the four messages.

cards.q: In what order are local objects destroyed?
cards.a:
In the reverse of the order they were constructed

The last object created is the first destroyed, so later objects can safely depend on earlier ones.

cards.q: When is a temporary object destroyed?
cards.a:
At the end of the full statement that created it

A temporary lives until the end of the full statement (the `;`), unless it is bound to a `const&`, which extends its life.

cards.q: When does a class need a destructor you write yourself?
cards.a:
When it holds a resource that must be released, such as a file

Members that manage themselves need no help. A hand-written destructor is for releasing something the class acquired.

cards.q: Are an object's members still valid inside its destructor's body?
cards.a:
Yes, the body runs first and the members are destroyed afterwards

The destructor body can still use every member; they are destroyed, in reverse order, after it finishes.
